analysis.investment_thesis: Craftsman Automation is a capital-intensive auto-components manufacturer burdened with debt/equity of 1.09x, finance costs of INR 217 Cr that nearly match net profit of INR 201 Cr, and two consecutive years of negative free cash flow (INR -115 Cr in FY24, INR -706 Cr in FY25). At 52.2x earnings and 6.1x book, the market is pricing a business I find financially precarious as though it were a quality compounder.
key_strengths: Revenue has compounded at 22.8% over eight years (INR 1,102 Cr to INR 5,690 Cr), demonstrating genuine market share gains across powertrain, aluminium, and industrial segments
Operating cash flow has been positive all five years (INR 283–608 Cr), confirming the core operating business generates real cash before financing
Diversified customer base across CVs, tractors, two-wheelers, and industrial/warehousing reduces single-sector cyclicality
key_risks: Debt/equity of 1.09x breaches my absolute maximum of 0.5x; borrowings surged from INR 1,755 Cr to INR 3,311 Cr in a single year as total assets nearly doubled — a large leveraged acquisition with unproven returns
Finance costs of INR 217 Cr (FY25) against net profit of INR 201 Cr means the entire equity profit is consumed by interest payments; one bad quarter wipes out shareholder earnings entirely
Auto-components is a cyclical business; the combination of high leverage and declining net profit (INR 337 Cr in FY24 to INR 201 Cr in FY25, -40%) in a supposedly normal year is alarming
red_flags: Graham Number ≈ INR 2,050 (EPS ~INR 147, BVPS ~INR 1,269); stock at INR 7,691 is 3.75x that figure — the most extreme overvaluation in this set of five stocks
Negative free cash flow of INR -706 Cr in FY25 — the company is consuming capital faster than it generates it; this is financed by debt, not earnings
Net profit fell 40% year-over-year (FY24 to FY25) while debt nearly doubled; this is precisely the combination of factors that precedes a financial restructuring
analysis.detailed_analysis:
My first concern with Craftsman is the balance sheet. Borrowings of INR 3,311 Cr against equity of INR 3,030 Cr (D/E 1.09x) violates one of my most fundamental rules — that a manufacturing business must not owe more than 50 pence for every pound of shareholder equity. The FY25 surge in borrowings and assets clearly reflects a major acquisition; total assets leapt from INR 4,706 Cr to INR 8,266 Cr, financed largely by debt. The ROE of 9.4% and ROCE of 11.7% do not justify such leverage.

The income statement compounds these concerns: finance costs have grown from INR 90 Cr (FY17) to INR 217 Cr (FY25), while net profit of INR 201 Cr barely covers those charges. Free cash flow of INR -706 Cr in FY25 means the company is destroying value in cash terms. I apply a Graham Number test: √(22.5 × 147 × 1,269) ≈ INR 2,050. The stock at INR 7,691 demands I overpay by 275%. A cyclical, capital-hungry business with deteriorating profits and rising debt should trade at a steep discount to intrinsic value, not a massive premium.
